desc:
A grid of letters is given as an integer matrix board, and a dictionary as a list words in which every word is itself an array of letter codes. In both, 1 stands for a, 2 for b, and so on up to 26 for z.

A word is found if its letters can be read along a path that starts at any cell and moves one step at a time to the cell directly above, below, left or right, without using any cell twice in the same path. Return the indices (0-based) of all found words, in increasing order. The words in the dictionary are all different, and each word is checked independently of the others.

For example, for the board with rows cat, oer, dgs and the words cat, tag, cod, reg, coat the answer is [0, 2, 3].
constraints: 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 100 and all words are different
hints: Searching the grid once for every word works for a few words, but repeats a lot of work: words that start with the same letters walk the same paths.

Store all words in a trie (a tree keyed by letter codes). Start a DFS from every cell and descend the trie in step with the path, so one walk serves every word with the same prefix. A branch stops as soon as the next letter has no child in the trie.

Mark the end of each word in the trie with its index. When the DFS reaches such a node, record the index and clear the marker so that the word is reported once. Optionally delete trie nodes that have become empty, which makes the search faster as words are found.
editorial: Build a trie of the dictionary; each word-ending node remembers the index of its word. For each cell run dfs(r, c, node): look up the cell's letter among the children of node, stop if it is missing, report the word index if the child ends a word, then mark the cell visited and recurse into the four neighbours with the child as the new trie node. Unmark the cell when returning (backtracking).

This beats running a single-word search for each word, because all words with a common prefix share the walk along that prefix, and a path that cannot be a prefix of any word is cut at once. Pruning the trie (removing a child once its subtree holds no unreported words) shrinks the search as more words are found. The cost is bounded by the number of self-avoiding paths that follow a trie path, at most m * n * 3L-1, but realistic inputs are far smaller.
